clue.text: " Front door " means of getting into deep water?

parts.note: the main is an old poetic name for the open sea
an entrance is a way in to somewhere

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a grand front door is a way of landing oneself in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deep water' suggests trouble, but here it is simply the sea, the poetic MAIN; the pieces are read in the reverse of the clue's order.
explanation.definitionFit: The principal way into a building is its chief doorway at the front.

clue.text: Official order

explanation.definitionFit: A marshal is an officer in charge of ceremonies, and to marshal is to arrange or put in order.

clue.text: One to consider when showing ones' temper

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
to rate is to judge or regard

explanation.surface: Advice to think about someone who has lost their temper.
explanation.definitionFit: Being angry means openly displaying bad temper.

clue.text: Paid in rentes, perhaps, for dainties

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the other here
signals the letters may be arranged another way

parts.note: met, as in met the bill, means paid

explanation.surface: Someone pays for delicacies with income from French government bonds.
explanation.walkthrough: RENTES (French government stocks) rearranged by 'perhaps' gives ENTRES, with MET put 'in'.
explanation.definitionFit: Entremets are sweet side dishes or desserts, delicacies served between courses.

clue.text: Dame has the wrong backing

indicators.note: going backwards means the word is read from end to start

parts.note: a tort is a civil wrong in law

explanation.surface: An older lady supports a mistaken cause.
explanation.walkthrough: TROT is an old word for an old woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A trot is an archaic, unflattering term for an old woman or hag.

clue.text: Served, and paid the penalty

explanation.surface: Someone did their time and atoned for it.
explanation.definitionFit: Answered can mean sufficed or did the job, and to have answered for a crime is to have suffered the punishment.

clue.text: Direct steering with success in the old river

parts.note: to con (or conn) a ship is to direct its steering
a go can mean a success, as in make a go of it

explanation.surface: Navigating a boat well along a historic waterway.
explanation.walkthrough: The great African river was renamed the Zaire when this puzzle appeared, hence 'old'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Congo is a major African river, once briefly renamed Zaire.

clue.text: Perhaps carp about the back part being dowdy

indicators.note: one piece goes round the other

parts.note: a carp is an example of a fish
the rump is the hindquarters

explanation.surface: A complaint about one's rear end looking unfashionable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carp' looks like a verb meaning complain, but it is the fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Frumpish means drab and old-fashioned in dress.

clue.text: Communications may be behindhand

parts.note: behindhand suggests late, but these remarks are spoken behind one's hand

explanation.surface: A complaint that messages may arrive late.
explanation.definitionFit: Asides are remarks made privately, often whispered behind a raised hand.

clue.text: Responses about proverbial loud speakers?

parts.note: re is the Latin-derived word for concerning or about
the proverb says actions speak louder than words

explanation.surface: A question about how people react to noisy public-address loudspeakers.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'actions speak louder than words' makes deeds the loud speakers.
explanation.definitionFit: Replies or reactive behaviour given in return to something are synonyms.

clue.text: Annoys the criminals they betray

explanation.surface: Something irritates the crooks that informers give away.
explanation.walkthrough: NARK is British slang both for 'irritate' and for a police informer, someone who betrays fellow criminals.
explanation.definitionFit: To nark is British slang for to irritate, and narks are informers who give away crooks to the police.

clue.text: Observed, we hear, who did it

indicators.note: signals that the words are taken as they sound when spoken

parts.note: the reply to 'who did it?' could be 'he did'

explanation.surface: A detective's question about who committed the crime, overheard.
explanation.walkthrough: Answer the question 'who did it?' with 'he did', and say it out loud.
explanation.definitionFit: To have observed a rule or warning is to have taken notice of and obeyed it.

clue.text: In my view set in colour is improved

indicators.note: one piece is placed within the other, as a jewel is set in a mount

parts.note: red is a colour
'for me' means in my opinion

explanation.surface: An art critic decides a picture with colour added looks better.
explanation.definitionFit: Something reformed has been changed for the better, amended.

clue.text: Painter married in a ship

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the other here

parts.note: a liner is a passenger ship

explanation.surface: An artist weds aboard a vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: LIMNER is an old word for a painter, especially of portraits or miniatures.
explanation.definitionFit: A limner is an archaic term for an artist who paints portraits or illuminates manuscripts.

clue.text: Uses feet — in dances ?

explanation.surface: Someone stepping out at a ball.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is a link; measures are also stately dances.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who sizes things in imperial units gauges length, and measures were formal slow dances.

clue.text: Where tongues wag loudest

parts.note: tongues wagging suggests gossip, but the clapper of a bell is its tongue, swinging in a tower

explanation.surface: A remark about the place where gossip is noisiest.
explanation.definitionFit: Bell towers house bells whose clappers, called tongues, swing to ring them.

clue.text: Well I never Loose, and not in love

parts.note: fancy! is an exclamation of surprise
free means unattached

explanation.surface: An exclamation at someone being unattached and single.
explanation.definitionFit: Fancy-free describes someone unattached romantically, with no sweetheart.

clue.text: He trips after a second glass

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second
a tumbler is a drinking glass

explanation.surface: A man falls over after another drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who trips is one who loses footing and falls.

clue.text: Insensitive places for attacks .

parts.note: dead can mean numb, without feeling
sets means puts or places

explanation.surface: Unfeeling spots chosen for assaults.
explanation.walkthrough: A dead set is a determined attack or onslaught.
explanation.definitionFit: A dead-set is a resolute onslaught, so the plural means concerted assaults.

clue.text: Synopsis to think over

explanation.surface: Summarise and then reflect.
explanation.definitionFit: A digest is a summary, and to digest an idea is to ponder it.

clue.text: The man to compose a song of praise?

indicators.note: composing arranges these letters into a new order

explanation.surface: A question about who will write a hymn.
explanation.definitionFit: An anthem is a choral work or hymn honouring God or a nation.

clue.text: A wonderful example left by a poet

parts.note: a marvel is a wonder

explanation.surface: A poet left behind an amazing model.
explanation.walkthrough: Andrew Marvell was a 17th-century English poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Andrew Marvell wrote 'To His Coy Mistress' and other metaphysical verse.

clue.text: Note, with regret, quite a few are horrible

parts.note: G is a musical note
to rue is to regret
some means a fair number

explanation.surface: A remark, made sorrowfully, that a good many things are dreadful.
explanation.definitionFit: Something gruesome is ghastly and horrifying, especially through death or injury.

clue.text: Petty quarrel about the right fish

indicators.note: one piece goes round the other

parts.note: a spat is a minor argument
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A minor squabble over which fish is correct.
explanation.definitionFit: The sprat is a small silvery fish of the herring family.

clue.text: Pistol's world he would put to the sword

definitions.text: Pistol's world he would put to the sword

parts.words: Pistol's world he would put to the sword
parts.note: in Shakespeare's Merry Wives, Pistol says the world is his shellfish, which he with sword will open

explanation.surface: A reference to a swaggering Shakespearean character who would conquer the world by force.
explanation.walkthrough: Pistol is a braggart in Shakespeare; his line 'the world's mine oyster, which I with sword will open' is the source of the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Pistol calls the world a shellfish he will prise open with his blade, a bivalve.

clue.text: Judge in a W. German city

explanation.surface: A magistrate in a West German town.
explanation.definitionFit: A trier is one who tries cases, and Trier is a city on the Moselle in West Germany.

clue.text: Follow and honour your leader

parts.note: the OBE is a British honour, Order of the British Empire

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: An instruction to obey and respect whoever is in charge.
explanation.definitionFit: To obey is to comply with or abide by an order.

clue.text: Here's trouble undiluted!

indicators.note: to trouble is to disturb, so these letters are stirred up

explanation.surface: An announcement that pure difficulty has arrived.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheer means pure or unmixed, as in sheer folly.

clue.text: Roué and French composer in a row

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the other here

parts.note: a line is a row
Jacques Ibert was a French composer

explanation.surface: A rake and a French musician sit side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A roué is a dissolute man, a rake given to debauchery.

clue.text: Morsel — pretty bad for Mrs. — Carey's bird

indicators.note: the letters are spoiled, made into a different arrangement

explanation.surface: A tasty but rotten scrap is given to Mrs Carey's pet bird.
explanation.walkthrough: Storm petrels were known to sailors as Mother Carey's chickens.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors called the small seabirds that appear before storms Mother Carey's chickens.
